summary: Defines the SIP P-Served-User private header for the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem. It solves a problem between the S-CSCF and an application server on the ISC interface by identifying which user a request is being handled for.

eli5.summary: In a phone company's network, one server may ask another to do something for a specific customer. This note adds a label that says which customer the request is for.

subtitle: A private SIP header that tells an application server which user a request is really being handled for.

tldr.problem: In the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem, a server working on a call for a user must guess who that user is from the Request-URI or P-Asserted-Identity, which already mean something else. Forwarding and similar services break because of this.
tldr.mechanism: The P-Served-User header carries the identity of the served user, plus optional parameters for the session case (originating or terminating) and the registration state. Proxies add it only inside a trusted domain.
tldr.outcome: It gives the S-CSCF and application servers an explicit answer to 'who is being served', but it is only meant for closed trusted networks such as 3GPP IMS, not the open Internet.

facts.value: IANA SIP Parameters registry, Header Fields subregistry

today: RFC 5502 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8217 and RFC 8498. The header is documented as intended for closed trusted networks such as 3GPP IMS, not for general Internet use.

sections.title: Why a New Header Was Needed
sections.content:
The 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) uses SIP as its main signaling protocol. 3GPP found problems with linking a SIP application server (AS) into a call, and the way to fix them was a new P-header, defined under the procedures of RFC 3427.

RFC 5502 defines the P-Served-User header field. It conveys two things on the ISC (IMS Service Control) interface between the S-CSCF and an AS: the identity of the served user and the session case that applies to this communication session and application invocation.
sections.eli5: A phone network sometimes hands a call to a helper computer. The helper needs to know whose call it is, so this note invents a name tag for that.

sections.title: Served User and Session Case
sections.content:
The served user is the user whose service profile a proxy or AS looks up when an initial request arrives that is originated by, originated on behalf of, or terminated to that user. The profile holds preferences and permissions used while processing the request.

In IMS the S-CSCF is a SIP proxy that acts as registrar and handles originating and terminating session states for its users. The user profile it downloads from the HSS includes the initial Filter Criteria (iFC), which say whether a request must be sent to an AS. The session case separates originating from terminating calls and says whether the user is registered.

Today the served user is inferred. For an originating case it is read from P-Asserted-Identity. For a terminating case it is read from the Request-URI. The same inference is repeated at the AS.
sections.eli5: The served user is the person the helper is working for. Until now the helper had to guess from clues on the envelope, like a return address.

sections.title: Scenarios Where the Guess Fails
sections.content:
Reading the served user from P-Asserted-Identity or the Request-URI overloads those fields with a second meaning. Basic calls work. Forwarding-style services do not. The RFC walks through three scenarios.

  • Diversion, then more terminating services. User B's AS diverts a call by changing the Request-URI to C. When the call returns to the S-CSCF and goes to the next AS, that AS reads the Request-URI and wrongly decides the served user is C.
  • Diversion as a new originating leg. The AS adds an orig parameter to the topmost Route header so B's originating services run. The S-CSCF then reads P-Asserted-Identity and picks user A, not B.
  • Call out of the blue. A service wants a call to appear to come from user B while running the profile of service identity C. Both cannot be expressed through P-Asserted-Identity.

The two requirements that follow are that the served user identity can be conveyed on the ISC interface, and that the session case is conveyed with it.
sections.eli5: If a letter is forwarded, the helper reads the new address and thinks the letter is for someone else. The helper needs a note that still says who it was originally for.

sections.title: The P-Served-User Header
sections.content:
The header may be added to initial requests for a dialog and to standalone requests that travel between nodes in a Trust Domain for P-Served-User. Its value is an identity (name-addr or addr-spec) representing the served user.

Two optional parameters refine it. sescase is orig or term and says whether the request is originated by or destined for the served user. regstate is reg or unreg and says whether the request is for a registered or unregistered user. Generic parameters are also allowed.
sections.eli5: It is a name tag with two small stickers: one says whether the person is calling or being called, the other whether they have signed in.

sections.title: How Proxies Handle It
sections.content:
A proxy that supports the header MUST insert it only in initial requests for a dialog or standalone requests, and only if it can determine the served user and the next hop is in the same Trust Domain. Otherwise it MUST NOT insert it.

When a proxy receives the header from a trusted node, it MUST take the value as the served user for any operation that needs one. It MUST remove the header if it came from outside the Trust Domain, and also if the next hop is outside the Trust Domain, before forwarding.

Appendix A explains why History-Info (RFC 4244) is not a substitute: it records Request-URI history, cannot express the originating case, cannot say which entry is the served user, and has no way to carry the session case. The RFC notes the two headers can still appear in the same request.
sections.eli5: Only trusted helpers may write the name tag, and anyone leaving the trusted group must peel it off first.

sections.title: Trust Domain and Security
sections.content:
RFC 5502 says P-headers have limited applicability. The header is only for use inside a Trust Domain where nodes trust each other, and the served user information is only meaningful when securely received from a member. It lacks any indication of who determined the served user, so it must be assumed to be the Trust Domain. Because a served user usually has validity in one administrative domain, it is generally not suitable for inter-domain or Internet-wide use. A closed network like 3GPP IMS is the example deployment.

The environment is expected to protect integrity and confidentiality, sometimes with IPsec and sometimes by physical protection. If the header leaks out of the domain, user-sensitive information is revealed. So proxies MUST NOT insert it toward a hop outside the domain, and inside the domain they MUST NOT insert it unless they know a proxy on the route understands it. There is no automatic way to learn support. The Spec(T) defining the Trust Domain MUST require member nodes to understand the header.
sections.eli5: The name tag is private. It is fine inside the club, but it must not leave the clubhouse because it tells outsiders who is being helped.
